title: InfoSeek: Agentic Search via Hierarchical Constraint Synthesis
one_liner: A framework that turns web exploration into constraint puzzles, generating synthetic training data that teaches AI agents to search better.
lead: When an AI agent searches for information across many webpages, it has to decide which link to follow next and know when it has found what it needs. Training agents to do this well is hard because real research tasks are complex and most datasets do not capture that complexity. This paper introduces a method that builds training data by imagining research as a constraint-satisfaction puzzle — a set of problems nested inside each other, where solving the whole thing means satisfying constraints at multiple levels.

problem.h2: Why agentic search training fails today
paras: An LLM-agent trying to research a topic needs to visit webpages, read them, and decide what to search for next. The agent has to learn two things: which pages matter, and when it has gathered enough information to answer the original question. Today's training data either has simple lookup tasks (find one fact on one page) or fake research tasks that do not match how real research actually works. A naive approach tries training agents on random webpage collections, but that teaches them nothing useful — they learn to browse randomly, not to build a coherent research strategy.

Real research requires satisfying nested goals. You need facts from multiple pages, but some facts only make sense after you have found other facts. A dataset of tasks where everything is on one page, or where any page will do, misses this entirely.

callout.html: Existing datasets for training agentic search do not capture the nested, multi-source nature of real research tasks, so agents trained on them search badly.

panels.title: 1. A real research task
panels.viz_args: Find: topic A -> subtopic B -> fact C
panels.caption: Real research has nested goals: answer the main question requires finding intermediate facts first.

panels.title: 2. Pages form an exploration tree
panels.caption: Each webpage links to others. Following links creates a branching tree of possible research paths.

panels.title: 3. Constraints emerge at each level
panels.caption: Layers of constraints: which pages satisfy the main goal, which satisfy sub-goals, which are just noise.

panels.title: 4. Sample a subtree, blur the constraints
panels.caption: Pick a subset of the tree, add misleading links, record what makes a page relevant.

panels.title: 5. Training data: task + relevance labels
panels.caption: Each training instance is a task plus a relevance score for each page, reflecting the constraint layers.

steps.text: Pick any real webpage, call it the starting point.
Follow outgoing links, creating a tree of neighboring pages. Record constraints that connect each page to the goal.
Pick a subset of the tree and add backtracking constraints — false paths or misleading links.
Mix genuine and fake links, label which pages truly satisfy the nested goals.
Output a task, a set of webpages, and a relevance score for each based on the constraints.

object.h2: The one thing the paper changes
paras: InfoSeek generates training data by conceptualizing the search process as a constraint-satisfaction problem. Instead of collecting real research behavior or writing synthetic tasks by hand, it builds tasks algorithmically by unrolling a webpage tree and labeling pages by how many constraint levels they satisfy. This shifts the problem from hand-labeling tasks to automatically extracting the structure of real webpages.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: constraint satisfaction depth
hidden.name: constraint satisfaction depth
paras: Constraint satisfaction depth is a count of how many nested goals a single webpage can help you solve: if a page directly answers the top-level question, its depth is 1; if it only helps after you have already found other facts, its depth is 2 or higher. This matters because pages that satisfy multiple levels of constraints are the ones an agent must learn to find and rank by importance to solve complex research tasks.

InfoSeek estimates this depth by tracing backward through the webpage tree. It builds a tree by expanding outward from a seed page (the diffusion phase), then samples a subtree and counts how many levels of constraints each page satisfies (the retrospection phase). Pages that satisfy constraints at multiple levels get higher depth scores.

heat.caption: Darker cells have higher constraint-satisfaction depth, meaning they help satisfy more of the nested research goals.

reads.html: A page's constraint depth tells you how central it is to the research task. Pages high in the tree hierarchy satisfy more of the top-level constraints; pages deep in branches satisfy only specialized sub-problems.
Constraint satisfaction depth is computed during the retrospection phase by backtracking through the sampled subtree and counting how many constraint levels each page contributes to satisfying.

mechanism.h2: Why the method works: the causal chain
paras: The mechanism has three parts. First, real research has a tree structure — each query or sub-question leads to new webpages, which in turn suggest other searches. By building a tree of webpages from a seed page (diffusion), InfoSeek captures that structure. Second, not all pages are equally important. Some pages answer the core question, others provide context, and others are distractions. By labeling pages with their constraint satisfaction depth — how many levels of nested sub-goals they help solve — InfoSeek teaches an agent what matters. Third, real datasets contain both signal and noise. Pages that are easy to find are not always relevant; pages that are truly useful might require knowing what to search for. By adding backtracking constraints and mixing genuine and misleading links (retrospection), InfoSeek creates an agent-training challenge that matches reality.

The result is training data where each task reflects the actual complexity of multi-level research. An agent trained on this data learns two skills together: it learns which pages to trust by reading their content, and it learns to stop searching when it has satisfied the nested constraints. This is more realistic than random-link datasets (which do not teach a strategy) or single-page datasets (which do not teach multi-step reasoning).

stages.s: Follow outbound links to build a tree

math.words: relevance score for a page equals the number of constraint levels it helps satisfy, divided by the total depth of the tree, scaled by how many other pages also satisfy those constraints.
symbols: a score from 0 to 1 indicating how important the page is for solving the task
how many nested constraint levels this page helps satisfy (1, 2, 3, etc.)
the maximum depth of any constraint chain in the research tree
a small penalty (0 to 0.3) if the page contradicts constraints at other levels

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Consider a research tree with max depth of 3. The main question (depth 1) asks for facts about neural networks.
Page A directly answers the main question, satisfies depth-1 constraint: relevance_A = (1 / 3) * (1 - 0) = 0.33
Page B gives historical context needed to understand Page A, satisfies depths 1 and 2: relevance_B = (2 / 3) * (1 - 0) = 0.67
Page C is about a related but different topic, satisfies only depth 3 partially: relevance_C = (1 / 3) * (1 - 0.2) = 0.27
Page B is ranked highest because it helps satisfy more levels of the nested research goal.

math.note: The formula gives higher relevance scores to pages that satisfy more levels of nested constraints, teaching an agent which pages matter most for the overall research goal.

charts.title: Agent trained on random webpages
charts.note: Without nested structure in the training data, agents learn to search randomly and do not know when to stop.

charts.title: Agent trained on InfoSeek data
charts.note: Constraint-based training teaches agents to gather information from multiple sources and recognize when they have satisfied the research goal.

items.html: If you start diffusion from a page that is unusual or off-topic, the generated tree will not reflect typical research. The constraints derived will be skewed, producing training tasks that do not match real research patterns.
Automatically determining which pages satisfy which constraints is imperfect. If the labeling is wrong, agents learn to weight irrelevant pages highly, and their search quality degrades.

If the backtracking constraints and false links are trivial to spot, agents do not learn to be skeptical. Real research requires reading carefully to distinguish signal from noise; if training is too easy, agents will not develop that skill.

When seed pages are chosen to represent common research domains, constraint labeling is accurate, and false paths are subtle and plausible, agents learn multi-source search strategies that work on new research tasks they have never seen before.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny research task: given a question like 'How do neural networks learn from mistakes?', generate a tree of 20 webpages (or snippets) using InfoSeek's diffusion phase. Manually label a few pages as satisfying depth-1, depth-2, and depth-3 constraints. Train an agent (a language model or retrieval system, for instance) on this synthetic task. Test it on a separate task with the same structure. Measure: (a) how many of the top pages the agent retrieves are truly central to the research goal (precision), and (b) how many of the actually central pages it finds (recall).
demo.closing: The demo must show that agents trained on InfoSeek-generated data retrieve more central pages and use fewer searches to satisfy the nested constraints than agents trained on random webpages.
